subject: history_social
passage: Marcus Licinius Crassus, the richest man in Rome in the first century BCE, built much of his fortune, according to the biographer Plutarch, on the city's frequent fires. Rome had no public fire service, and its crowded timber buildings burned often. Crassus assembled several hundred enslaved builders and architects and, when a fire broke out, hurried to the scene with them. He did not begin by fighting the flames. Instead, he offered to buy the burning building and those next to it, and the owners, watching their property disappear, usually accepted a fraction of its worth. Only once the sale was agreed did his men put out the fire and rebuild. Plutarch adds, with evident disapproval, that in this way much of Rome came into Crassus's hands.
stem: According to the text, how did Crassus profit from fires in Rome?

choices.A: He put out fires quickly and then sold the rescued buildings back to their owners.
choices.B: He bought burning buildings and their neighbors at low prices before his men put out the flames.
choices.C: He charged property owners a large fee for the services of his firefighters.
choices.D: He trained enslaved builders and hired them out to rebuild the city after fires.

explanation.why: The text describes the sequence: Crassus "did not begin by fighting the flames" but offered to buy the burning building and those beside it; desperate owners "accepted a fraction of its worth"; and "only once the sale was agreed" did his men put out the fire and rebuild. The profit came from buying cheaply before extinguishing.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the order: the purchase came first, and nothing suggests he sold buildings back to their owners.
explanation.B: Correct. He bought the burning building and its neighbors at a fraction of their worth and only then had the fire put out.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions a fee for firefighting; Crassus bought the property.
explanation.D: Incorrect. His men rebuilt the property he had bought; the text says nothing about hiring them out.
